newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon is criticized on Gulf War chemicals.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon is criticized on Gulf War chemicals.

text.p: The Defence Department came under sharp attack at a Senate hearing on Wednesday for not admitting until last week that thousands of U.S. troops in the 1991 Gulf War might have been exposed to dangerous chemicals.

The Pentagon said last Thursday that as many as 5,000 soldiers might have been in range of nerve gas from an Iraqi ammunition dump that was blown up by U.S. troops a few days after the war ended. The previous estimate was that 1,100 soldiers might have been at risk.

The Pentagon said it still had no evidence of any illnesses caused by Iraqi chemical weapons despite thousands of complaints of fatigue and pain from soldiers who served in the Gulf and birth defects in some of their children born after the war.

But several senators at the hearing of the Intelligence and Veterans Affairs committees said the Defence Department had been slow to respond to reports of the so-called Gulf War syndrome and was refusing to admit the seriousness of the problem.

"I am convinced that the attitude of 'No problem, and e're going to prove it' pervades the DOD thinking and management of this public health mystery," Sen. Jay Rockefeller, D-West Virginia, said. He urged President Clinton to appoint new health officials at the department.
"The issue is a shameful campaign of obstruction and delay," added Sen. Richard Shelby, R-Alabama.
"Is it any wonder that our Persian Gulf veterans question the Pentagon's credibility and strongly suspect a coverup?" Sen. Paul Wellstone, D-Minnesota, asked.

John McLaughlin of the Central Intelligence Agency said the CIA had determined from an intelligence review that Iraq did not use chemical or biological weapons during the war. But he said the release of chemicals from the destruction of an Iraqi bunker in March 1991 could have contaminated an area up to 25 kms (15 miles) from the site.

McLaughlin said containers in that and another bunker were not marked and it was not known until earlier this year that they contained nerve gas. He said the CIA was trying to find out if there was any other exposure to chemicals.
"We're working this very hard, almost around the clock," he said.

Stephen Joseph, assistant defence secretary for health affairs, and Kenneth Kizer, under secretary of the Department of Veterans Affairs, said their departments were aggressively investigating the health problems of Gulf War veterans.

"VA encourages all Persian Gulf War veterans, whether symptomatic or not, to avail themselves of the Gulf War Registry examination programme, especially if they are concerned about possible exposure to chemical warfare agents in light of DOD's recent announcements," Kizer said.
Deputy Defence Secretary John White told another Senate committee that he had ordered a review of all aspects of the Pentagon's medical research and investigations of specific incidents.
White said in a letter to Strom Thurmond, the South Carolina Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, that he directed the Army to conduct an inquiry into the chemical release.
